texts: Ventricular Tumors: Microsurgical Anatomy & Lateral Approaches
Surgical corridors, neurovascular orientation, and operative strategies for lateral ventricular pathology.
Incidence and Primary vs. Secondary Classification
Pecker Schema: Primary tumors originate within the lining; secondary lesions invade across ventricular boundaries.
The Symptom Triad of Ventricular Neoplasms
Fontanelle Tension: Full or bulging anterior fontanelle.
Developmental Signs: Failure to thrive and milestone loss.
Hakim-like Triad: Gait instability, dementia, and headache.
Cognitive Changes: Short-term memory consolidation loss.
Intracranial Pressure: Positional nausea and papilledema.
Tectal lesions cause rapid noncommunicating hydrocephalus via sylvian aqueduct stenosis.
Up-Gaze Paralysis: Dorsal midbrain tectal compression.
Collier Sign: Retraction of upper eyelids.
Diagnostic Biomarkers: CSF and serum AFP / β-hCG testing.
Therapeutic Sensitivity: Exquisite response to radiation.
Rapid Involution: Tumor shrinkage and chiasm relief.
CSF Diversion vs. Direct Tumor Resection
Young, medically fit patients where tumor extirpation restores natural CSF channels permanently.
Medically frail elderly patients with obstructive hydrocephalus: ETV or shunt safely resolves symptoms.
Directing craniotomy toward the arterial pedicle allows early devascularization before debulking.
Arterial Inflow: Distinguishes choroidal feeders from normal branches.
Mixed Phase: Reveals tumor capillary blush and nidus boundaries.
Venous Outflow: Delineates drainage into internal cerebral veins.
Density: Highest in posterior frontal and parietal regions.
Infarction Risk: Sacrifice leads to venous hemorrhagic necrosis.
Strategy: Transcortical approach when bridging is dense.
Drainage: Dominant inferolateral temporal venous conduit.
Traction Danger: Subtemporal retraction causes venous rupture.
Sequelae: Wernicke region infarction and severe aphasia.
The Five Sectors of the Lateral Ventricle
The Five Segments of the Fornix
Frontal horns contain zero choroid plexus; the anterior septal vein serves as the primary orientation beacon.
Medial Wall: Transparent septum pellucidum leaves.
Lateral Wall: Bulging head of the caudate nucleus.
Roof & Floor: Genu and rostrum of corpus callosum.
Distance Posterior to the Foramen of Monro
Anastomosis of anterior septal and thalamostriate veins entering the internal cerebral vein.
The genu of the internal capsule lies directly lateral to the venous angle within the lateral ventricular wall.
Overaggressive lateral coagulation or traction at the striothalamic junction risks irreversible hemiplegia.
Natural cleft between thalamus and fornix harboring the choroid plexus and medial posterior choroidal branches.
Roof: Body of the corpus callosum.
Lateral Wall: Slender body of caudate nucleus.
Floor: Dorsal thalamus and forniceal body.
Anatomic Elements of the Ventricular Trigone
Atrial tumors frequently entrap the occipital horn, creating an isolated expanding fluid-filled cyst.
Asymmetry: Most anatomically variable ventricular sector.
Choroid Status: Devoid of choroid plexus lining.
Floor Boundary: Defined inferiorly by collateral trigone.
Internal Cerebral Veins vs. Basal Vein
Tributaries: Anterior septal, caudate, and thalamostriate veins.
Course: Dorsal roof inside the velum interpositum.
Termination: Converge behind splenium into Vein of Galen.
Tributaries: Inferior choroidal, inferior ventricular, amygdaloid veins.
Course: Wraps around the midbrain in ambient cistern.
Rule: Preservation imperative to avoid diencephalic stroke.

Arterial Landmark: Trace pericallosal arteries beneath cingulate.

Clinical Deficit: Severe akinetic mutism and abulia.
